en: The *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* translated by the Western Jin layman Nie Daozhen.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus, including the elders Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahākātyāyana, who were the foremost among such a multitude;
furthermore, there were sixteen bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with Maitreya as their leader among the thousand bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa;
and there were also one thousand two hundred bodhisattvas from other directions, with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva as their leader.
At that time, during the final watch of the night, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called "All-Illuminating Light.

Having entered this samādhi, his entire body emitted a golden radiance; the light was so intense that it illuminated the Jeta Grove as if it were made of gold. It circled and turned back, shining upon Mañjuśrī’s chamber and transforming it into seven tiers of golden terraces. Upon each terrace were five hundred transformation Buddhas, walking to and fro within the central space.

At that time, before the chamber of Mañjuśrī, five hundred lotus flowers made of the seven precious jewels spontaneously manifested. They were as large as chariot wheels, with stems of white silver and pedestals of *amṛta* agate; their filaments were composed of multicolored pearls. Light emanated from these flowers, illuminating the Buddha’s vihāra, then emerging from the vihāra and returning to enter the chamber of Mañjuśrī.

At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Bhadrapāla. When this auspicious omen appeared, Bhadrapāla immediately emerged from his chamber, paid homage at the Buddha’s vihāra, went to Ānanda’s chamber, and said to him:
“You should know the time; tonight the World-Honored One will manifest signs of supernatural power and preach the wondrous Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings. You must strike the *gandī*.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed him, saying:
"O Great Being!
The World-Honored One has now entered a profound meditative concentration; since he has not yet issued a command, how can the assembly be gathered?"
When these words were spoken, Śāriputra went to Ānanda and said to him:
"Brother in Dharma!
It is time to assemble the community."
At that time, Ānanda entered the Buddha’s vihāra and paid homage to the Buddha; before he had even raised his head, a voice in the air addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Quickly assemble the community of monks."

Having heard this, Ānanda was filled with great joy; he struck the *gandī* to assemble the community, and the sound of it resounded throughout Śrāvastī, reaching as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Then Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, together with countless sons of gods, took celestial flowers and incense and proceeded to the Jeta Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and immediately smiled; five-colored light issued forth from the Buddha’s mouth, and as this light emerged, the Jetavana Monastery was transformed into lapis lazuli.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, entered the Buddha’s vihāra and paid homage to the Buddha. From each of his knees there grew five lotus flowers. When Mañjuśrī joined his palms before the Buddha, from the tips of his ten fingers and the lines of his palms, ten thousand golden lotuses emerged, which he scattered over the Buddha. These transformed into a great canopy of the seven precious gems, suspended with various banners and streamers. Within the canopy, immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions appeared. Having circumambulated the Buddha three times, they withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has already personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; he performs Buddha-works here in this Sahā world and manifests with sovereign mastery throughout the ten directions, yet after a long period of time, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
“This Mañjuśrī possesses great compassion; he was born in this land in the village of Tālaka, into the family of the brahmin Brahmadeva.”

At the time of his birth, the house and dwelling within the home transformed into a lotus flower. He emerged from his mother’s right side with a body the color of purple gold; as soon as he touched the ground, he was able to speak like a celestial youth, and a canopy of the seven treasures followed him, covering him above.

He went to various seers seeking the method of renunciation; yet none among the ninety-five kinds of Brahmins or the masters of debate were able to respond to him. Only by leaving the household life and training in the Way under me did he dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. By the power of this samādhi, he manifests—in the ten directions—either his initial birth, his renunciation, his passing away, his entry into parinirvāṇa, or the distribution of his relics, thereby benefiting sentient beings.

This Great Being shall dwell long in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Four hundred and fifty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he will go to the Snowy Mountains and proclaim and expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras for five hundred seers. He will teach and mature these five hundred seers, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression. Assuming the appearance of a bhikṣu among the various celestial beings, he will fly through the air to his native land. Beneath a nyagrodha tree in a wilderness marsh, he will sit cross-legged and enter the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. By the power of this samādhi, golden light will issue from all the pores of his body; this light will pervasively illuminate the worlds of the ten directions, delivering those with whom he has a karmic connection. Each of the five hundred seers will see fire issuing from the pores of his body.

At that time, Mañjuśrī’s body was like a mountain of purple gold; he stood exactly sixteen feet tall, adorned with a radiant halo, each face spanning one fathom. Within this halo were five hundred transformation Buddhas, and each transformation Buddha had five transformation Bodhisattvas serving as attendants.

Mañjuśrī’s crown was adorned with Vaiḍūrya jewels of five hundred colors; within each color, the sun, moon, stars, the palaces of devas and nāgas, and all rare wonders seen by sentient beings in the world were all manifested.
The white tuft of hair between his brows curls to the right, from which emanate transformation Buddhas that enter into a net of light.

The radiance of his entire body blazes forth in successive flames; within each flame are five maṇi jewels, and each maṇi jewel possesses its own distinct light with clearly defined colors. Among these manifold colors, the transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are beyond full description.

With his left hand holding an almsbowl and his right hand supporting a Mahāyāna sūtra, once he had manifested this appearance, the light and flames were all extinguished, and he transformed into a statue of lapis lazuli.
Upon his left arm were ten Buddha seals; within each seal were ten Buddha images, and the names of the Buddhas were spoken with perfect clarity.
Upon his right arm are the seals of the seven Buddhas; within each seal are seven Buddha images, and the names of the seven Buddhas are clearly and distinctly visible.
Within the heart region of his body is an image of pure gold, seated in the full lotus posture, exactly six feet in height upon a lotus flower, manifesting in all four directions.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

“This Mañjuśrī possesses immeasurable supernatural powers and immeasurable transformations that cannot be fully recorded; I shall now speak of them briefly for the sake of sentient beings who are blind and ignorant in future ages. If there are sentient beings who merely hear the name of Mañjuśrī, they will eliminate the karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over twelve hundred million kalpas.
If they prostrate to him and make offerings, they will be born into the families of all Buddhas in every successive life, protected by the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.”

Therefore, sentient beings should diligently fix their mindfulness upon the image of Mañjuśrī. Regarding the method for mindful recollection of Mañjuśrī’s image: first, one should recollect an image made of lapis lazuli. As previously described, one should contemplate each detail until they are all clearly perceived.

If one has not yet attained this vision, one should recite and uphold the Śūraṅgama [Dhāraṇī] and invoke the name of Mañjuśrī for one to seven days; Mañjuśrī will certainly come to that person's abode.

Furthermore, if there are those with karmic obstructions from past lives who see [Mañjuśrī] in a dream, those who see him in a dream will, within their present bodies, if they seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, attain the stage of srotāpanna up to anāgāmin because of having seen Mañjuśrī.
If those who have left the household life see Mañjuśrī, by virtue of having seen him, they shall become arhats in a single day and night.
If there are those with deep faith in the Vaipulya sūtras, this Prince of Dharma will, within their state of meditative concentration, expound the profound Dharma for them.
"For those with much distracted minds, he will explain the true meaning within their dreams, causing them to become firm and attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"If anyone thinks of this Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, or wishes to make offerings and cultivate meritorious deeds, he will immediately manifest a transformation body as a poor, solitary, and suffering sentient being and appear before that practitioner."
If there are those who wish to contemplate Mañjuśrī, they should practice a mind of loving-kindness; for one who practices loving-kindness shall see Mañjuśrī.

Therefore, the wise should carefully observe the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of Mañjuśrī. By making such an observation, through the power of Śūraṅgama, they shall swiftly behold Mañjuśrī.
To practice this contemplation is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among all sentient beings, those who hear the name of Mañjuśrī or behold his image shall not fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the name of Mañjuśrī, even if they possess heavy karmic obstructions, they shall not fall into the extreme and fierce fires of Avīci; they will always be born in pure lands in other directions, meet the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When these words were spoken, five hundred bhikṣus became free from dust and defilement, attaining arhatship; immeasurable devas gave rise to the bodhicitta, vowing to always follow Mañjuśrī.
At that time, Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for these relics of Mañjuśrī, who shall erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances over them?”
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"There are eight great spirits on Mount Gandhamādana who shall personally carry it away and place it upon the summit of the Vajra Mountain in the Fragrant Mountains. Immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and spirits will constantly come to make offerings. When the great assembly gathers, the image will always emit light; that light will expound the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and so forth."
Bhadrapāla! This son of the Dharma has attained an indestructible body; I now speak to you, so you should receive and uphold it well, and extensively proclaim it for the sake of all sentient beings.

When these words were spoken, the great bodhisattvas such as Bhadrapāla, the great śrāvakas such as Śāriputra, and the eight classes of beings including devas and nāgas, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Parinirvāṇa of Mañjuśrī.
